extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and experimental natural philosophers (practitioners of observational astronomy and optics)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and practical standards for making and reporting astronomical observations, determining planetary orbits, and conducting optical experiments (prism/colour/refraction) with rigorous controls and instrumentation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for orbital-determination method
rubrics_metrics.description: “where, besides observations, nothing more is supposed, than that the orbits of the planets be elHptical, that the sun be in their common focus, and in fine, that their periods be discovered in such a manner as that no sensible error can arise, at least in two or three revolutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and make explicit the minimal geometric/physical assumptions before applying the construction: assume elliptic orbits, sun at common focus, and that periods are known accurately (so that no sensible error arises over two or three revolutions). Do not build on additional unsupported suppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive orbit from three heliocentric places
rubrics_metrics.description: Method showing how "from three heliocentric places of a planet, and the observed distances from the sun, its orbit may be described; which formerly required five such observations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric construction (hyperbolas whose transverse diameters equal differences of distances, intersection gives other focus) or the analytic quadratic reduction described to recover transverse diameter and foci distance. Emphasize that three well-chosen heliocentric places plus distances suffice where previous methods needed five observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure using Mars oppositions to determine distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe Mars in opposition (sun, earth, Mars aligned) and then after subsequent returns (e.g., after 68 days Mars returns to same point while earth's return interval differs); observe longitudes of sun and Mars to give all angles of triangle PBS and thereby compute distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule and record observations at oppositions and after defined time intervals; measure longitudes precisely to derive triangle sides and angles; then apply the geometric/analytic steps outlined (triangles KSL, KLP, LSP etc.) to determine planet-sun distances and orbit parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational measurement practice for sunspots
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephemeris “reduced from careful observations, made with the micrometer, of the distances of the spots from the limb of the sun, and the differences of altitudes and azimuths from the upper and under parts and sides of him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calibrated micrometers to measure distances from solar limb, record altitudes and azimuths differences from multiple parts of the spot; when a spot is broken into pieces, record the middle of the spot or the middle of the larger piece as the reference. Produce a daily ephemeris reduced from careful measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-site comparison to validate observations
rubrics_metrics.description: “The comparing of the observations made in two distant places, Greenwich and Oxford, evince the diligence of the observers, and the goodness of their instruments; the differences between them being easily excusable; for that the spot had a diameter more considerable than any of the differences, and was broken into several pieces.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare independent observations from geographically separated observers to assess diligence and instrument quality. Expect and document small differences; evaluate whether differences are explainable by instrument resolution or object structure (e.g., spot diameter and fragmentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescope/glass sizing by observational purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Borelli’s offer: furnish societies with three very good glasses: one of 10 or 12 feet for a chamber; another of 25 or 30 feet for ordinary observations; and a third of 60 or 80 feet for making new discoveries. Private persons may use glasses of 14 or 20 feet to observe eclipses of Jupiter's satellites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select telescope focal length according to intended use: small indoor/chamber work (10–12 ft), routine observations (25–30 ft), deep/new-discovery work (60–80 ft), and mid-size (14–20 ft) adequate for precise timings such as eclipses of Jupiter's satellites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Jupiter-satellite eclipses for longitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Eclipses of Jupiter's satellites “happen almost daily, and afford so fair a way for establishing the longitudes over all the earth. ... the emersion and immersion ... is so momentary and so sensible, that they may be observed with the greatest exactness, being altogether exempt from those essential inconveniencies that accompany the eclipses of the sun and moon ... whose beginning and end are always doubtful, by reason of a certain ambiguous light.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer timings of Jupiter-satellite eclipses for longitude determination because they are frequent, brief, sharp events and less affected by ambiguous light than solar or lunar eclipse timings. Use appropriate mid-size instruments for these observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit apparatus and conditions in optical experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucas describes apparatus details (prism vertical angle 60°, distance to wall ~18 ft, hole diameter ~1/8 inch, prism 2 inches from hole), equal refractions on both sides, refraction power computed by ratio of sines 2 to 3, room darkened to like darkest night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report exact apparatus geometry and experimental conditions (angles, distances, aperture sizes, computed refractive indices, ambient illumination) so others can reproduce and evaluate the experiment. Quantify values and note how they were varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control, replication, and blind observation to avoid bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucas ran many trials, varied conditions (clear day vs bright cloud), added second and third refractions, and “called into the room some unconcerned persons, wholly ignorant what the experiment aimed at; and demanding whether they saw not the coloured silks and ruler in a crooked line ? they answered in the negative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct multiple trials across varying conditions, add or remove optical stages to isolate effects, and use uninformed/independent observers to check for expectation bias. Replicate results under different configurations to confirm robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable predictions as tests of theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucas lays out predicted observable consequences of Newton's unequal refrangibility (e.g., in a microscope two differently coloured silks should appear with different degrees of brightness or blur; in water the coloured silks should not appear in a straight line), then reports whether these predicted effects occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate concrete, observable predictions from a theory and design experiments that would reveal those effects. If the predicted effects are absent under controlled tests, treat that as substantive evidence against the theory (or as indication of additional factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing ambient/contingent influences on spectra
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments with a paper circle and prism showed the coloured image on the retina changed posture depending on whether the circle was backed by shutter or open air; Lucas infers that "the present situation and order of colours arise not from any intrinsical property of refrangibility ... but from contingent and extrinsical circumstances of neighboring objects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether neighbouring illumination and background alter the observed spectrum; if so, account for environmental scattering/reflection when interpreting spectral ordering or extent. Design experiments to isolate intrinsic refrangibility from ambient-light effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing 'primary' colours by filtration/stacking media
rubrics_metrics.description: Covering the shutter hole with thin slices of ivory produced yellow transmitted light which, on adding more slices, became red; Lucas concludes that "yellowness of light is not a primary colour, but a compound of red, &c."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use filters/stacked translucent media to see whether a perceived colour persists as a primary or changes compositionally; interpret changes as evidence for compound nature. Record incremental changes as media are added/removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document negative or inconclusive results and experimental limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucas repeatedly notes failures to detect predicted effects (e.g., no unequal focus in microscope, colored silks seen in a straight line through water/refractions), and mentions intervening difficulties when experiments could not be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report negative results, failed attempts, and experimental difficulties alongside successful trials. Note instrument or observational limitations (e.g., high sun, fineness of spot) that may prevent precise measurements, so readers can judge reliability.
